item.title: A drought-starved reservoir in the Southwest "drank" 60 feet of water in weeks and then ...
item.summary: The clearest proof comes from space. Landsat 9 satellite images taken on September 20 and November 7 show Navajo Reservoir's surface area expanding ...
item.page_text:
For most of 2026, Navajo Reservoir sat at 60 percent of its average capacity — a quiet symptom of the heat, snow drought, and long-term water stress that had come to define the Four Corners region. Then, between late September and early November, satellites watched something that didn’t fit the pattern .
In less than two months, the lake rose nearly 60 feet.
What happened across northern New Mexico, southern Colorado, and the broader Four Corners in those weeks was striking — and deeply contradictory .
The clearest proof comes from space. Landsat 9 satellite images taken on September 20 and November 7 show Navajo Reservoir’s surface area expanding dramatically — a visual record of a lake swallowing nearly 60 feet (18 meters) of water in weeks.
By November 7, the reservoir stood at 108 percent of its average capacity for that date. Compare that to the 60 percent recorded on September 20, and the turnaround is almost hard to process. That November reading also marked the highest water level at Navajo since August 2019 — seven years of deficit, partially erased in under two months. The Bureau of Reclamation had reduced releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17, setting a lower baseline heading into the storm events. Even so, the scale of the rise was extraordinary.
To understand why this transformation felt so jarring, you have to understand what the Four Corners region — spanning southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico — had been living through.
Long-term drought had stressed the area for years. Winter 2025–26 then brought a snow drought across the West, stripping away the reliable spring snowmelt that typically replenishes reservoirs like Navajo. High temperatures in 2026 compounded the damage, leaving soils dry and water supplies strained heading into fall.
Against that backdrop, what the storms delivered was almost surreal. From early September through early November, precipitation totals across the Four Corners ran 2 to 4 times the seasonal average . A region quietly drying out was suddenly overwhelmed with water it had no infrastructure — and no landscape — ready to absorb.
The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers surged with runoff as the storms moved through. Communities along their banks paid a steep price.
Pagosa Springs, Colorado — about 40 miles northeast of Navajo Reservoir — was among the hardest hit. The first storm event alone dropped 5.05 inches of rain on the town. On October 23, the San Juan River reached major flood stage. After a second round of rain, the river spiked again on November 1, climbing near the catastrophic record set during a devastating 1911 flood. Officials issued evacuation orders, responders rescued dozens of people, and streets flooded across a region that had spent years praying for moisture.
The flooding wasn’t limited to Pagosa Springs. It was regional in scope, touching communities across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico.
The same storms that forced evacuations also delivered something the region had been waiting years for: meaningful drought relief.
Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, built from satellite data and ground-based observations, tracked steady improvements through the fall. The group’s November 3 summary put it plainly: “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin.”
That declaration carries an important qualifier. Long-term drought persists across parts of the Southwest despite weeks of heavy rain. Storms can recharge a reservoir and ease surface conditions, but they can’t erase years of accumulated deficit in groundwater, soil moisture, and snowpack. The same rainfall that rescued Navajo Reservoir also flooded surrounding communities. Water arrived — just not on anyone’s terms.
So why did this happen now, and why so intensely?
Wet weather in the Southwest has historically been linked to El Niño events, when the equatorial jet stream strengthens and steers moisture-laden storms inland. The autumn 2026 system fit that pattern — but with amplifying factors. Experts noted that the low-pressure system tracked at an unusually low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from anomalously warm ocean temperatures off the California coast.
A strengthening El Niño pattern is currently underway, raising the likelihood of more such storms being funneled across the Southwest interior in the months ahead. The combination of El Niño dynamics and record-warm sea-surface temperatures appears to have intensified what might otherwise have been a significant but unremarkable fall storm season — producing something rarer: a weather event capable of rewriting a reservoir’s seven-year record while simultaneously pushing rivers toward century-old flood benchmarks.
What the Four Corners experienced wasn’t simply a drought ending. It was a reminder that in an arid region under increasing climate stress, water doesn’t return gradually — it arrives all at once, and rarely on schedule.

item.title: Search the Planet with AI
item.summary: The satellite image above shows an area of recent deforestation in the Amazon. I found this example using a new satellite imagery search tool from Planet, which allows you to search the Earth using nothing more complicated than a natural-language description. Machine learning has been used to search satellite imagery for patterns and geographical features for quite some time. Around a decade ago projects such as Terrapattern and Descartes Labs' GeoVisual Search (both now in the dead pool) demonstrated how computers could scan enormous collections of satellite images to find visually similar features. Now Planet Labs has brought this idea back in a rather more ambitious form with Planet AI . Its new application allows you to describe what you are looking for in ordinary language and then searches a global index of satellite imagery for matching locations. Instead of having to know the coordinates of somewhere you want to investigate, or manually scan satellite images looking for something interesting, you can simply ask Planet AI to find it for you.
